editions.body:
# The Small Moon Rose First

## Day 617

Nell cut the six hundred seventeenth notch into her belt while the Glass Gate cracked above her.

The knife skipped. A new white line opened across the old leather, crooked but countable. Behind her, the last living resistance fighters kept their palms against the copper rails. Their breath came in ragged chorus. The rails carried the magic they gave into the panes, and the glass shaped it into a doorway full of winter stars.

It was not enough. A black thread ran from the shattered ledger room, through the arch, and around Bash's left shoulder. Words crawled inside it: fragments of given names, family names, homes spoken by frightened mouths. Somewhere beyond the fallen stone, the Hollow Regent was still alive and pulling.

“Five seconds,” Bash said. He had one hand in the light and the other locked around Nell's wrist. “I can hold the return path.”

“You said that five seconds ago.”

“Those were experimental seconds.”

Even now, he could make annoyance elbow past terror. He was the brother Ravel had assigned her without paperwork, younger by a year and older by several disasters.

At the foot of the hill, Saint screamed and tried to bite the blue sparks off his own bridle. Tavra dragged the gray mule toward the trees. Her free hand was lifted in farewell.

Trenn should have been there to shout at them. One word, then stop, the road guide had taught them. Give the Regent's people one piece of yourself and make them spend blood finding the rest. But Trenn lay behind the broken primary ledger, and the copper gaming token he had left them was split into two rough crescents. One cut Nell's palm. The other shone between Bash's fingers.

The black thread tightened. Bash's shoulder jerked toward the arch.

“It's using you as a road,” Nell said.

“I know.”

“Then let go.”

“Absolutely not.”

The small blue moon cleared the ridge. Eleven minutes before the large gold one, exactly as Bash had once made her stay awake all night to prove.

That blue light touched the Gate. Nell felt her own remembered departure sharpen inside the charged glass: freezer air, a red hoodie, her mother's hand slipping from hers. Bash's living memory burned beside it, private and different. They had never told each other the dates. In Ravel, dates could become handles too.

The Regent's thread reached the skin below Bash's ear.

Nell had rehearsed the severance line until the Gate Cant lived under her tongue. It could cut a path. It could not aim a traveler, choose a time, or put a broken road back together.

She made the choice anyway.

“Living road, release the held path!”

Her breath supplied the final living push. The Cant shaped it through the resistance's stored charge. The bright path between their hands snapped.

Bash's fingers slid from her wrist. Nell caught skin, then his half-token, then nothing.

“I'm right behind you,” he shouted.

The glass-light folded around her before she could decide whether to believe him.

## February 18

Nell hit a freezer door hard enough to make every pizza behind it jump.

Someone screamed. A shopping basket overturned. Frost smoked around Nell's red sleeves, and an untied sneaker skidded in a crushed bag of peas.

Her body was thirteen again. The Gate had returned the narrow shoulders and too-short jeans of her departure, but it had kept the pale ash-hound tracks around her calf and the shiny ridge across her palm. Her tally belt hung twice around her waist. The copper crescent was still clenched in her fist.

Celia seized both her arms.

“Nell? Nell, where did you go?”

Her mother was wearing the same worried expression, holding the same carton of eggs. The freezer clock had advanced eleven seconds.

At the hospital, staff photographed scars that had healed months before they appeared. They found old fractures, calluses, and a body half-starved by a place no scan could locate. They found no trace of Bash.

The calendar still said February 18.

The supermarket cameras made the eleven seconds worse. Nell watched herself stand beside Celia in one frame, reaching for a freezer handle. In the next, the aisle was empty except for her falling basket. Eleven seconds later she struck the glass from the wrong direction, wearing the same clothes around a body that had learned too many new ways to flinch.

There was no flare, no second silhouette, no shadow shaped like a Gate. The footage proved that something had happened and refused to prove the part that mattered.

That first week, Nell slept beneath the kitchen table because it had three solid sides. She woke with her hand curled around a knife that was no longer on her belt. Celia started announcing herself before entering rooms. Neither of them called this improvement.

Celia believed that Nell had vanished. She believed the injuries and the panic when a metal cart squealed like a Drosswall arrow. Believing in Sebastian was harder.

They searched anyway. Sebastian, twelve years old. Boston, perhaps Cambridge. Cello lessons. Latin good enough to insult a customs priest in two dead declensions. No surname. No exact home. No date on which he had disappeared.

Celia phoned missing-child lines while Nell searched recital programs, school newsletters, and photographs of youth orchestras. Every dark-haired boy holding a cello stopped her breath. Every wrong face started it again. She found three Sebastians in Cambridge and nine around Boston. One played violin. One was six. One had moved away before Nell ever touched the freezer door.

There was no matching missing-child report. There was no boy with the right crooked little finger. There were only thousands of Sebastians and an increasingly gentle series of questions about whether Bash might have been someone Nell invented to survive.

On the fourth night, Nell laid her copper crescent beside the belt with its 617 cuts.

Dead was possible. Invented was not.

Missing, she decided, and opened Celia's laptop.

She made the post anonymous. She gave it no photograph and no real location. For the title she used a sentence that would mean nothing to a search engine and everything to one infuriating boy.

**The Small Moon Rose First.**

## The Facts Strangers Can Steal

For three weeks, nobody answered. In the fourth, everybody did.

Nell had posted too much at first: two moons, a place called Ravel, the Glass Gate, a gray mule, the glass arrows at Drosswall, Marn's Bridge. She mentioned a boy called Bash who played cello, knew Latin, and had survived 617 days beside her. The details felt useless until strangers copied them back with confidence.

One claimant sent a picture of a copper crescent filed from a plumbing washer. He knew the small moon was blue because Nell had written it. He knew about the arrows because a local reporter had repeated the story under a headline with the word *delusion* in it.

“What was under Marn's Bridge?” Nell asked on their video call.

“Treasure,” he said immediately. “The Regent's treasure. We were going to split it.”

Nell closed the call.

Under Marn's Bridge there had been thousands of stoppered jars. The glass itself had done nothing. Living clerks serving the Regent had pressed stolen identity-lines into it, and living victims had whispered from the stored magic when Bash and Nell carried the jars into daylight. Treasure did not beg you to remember its children.

The claimant sent six more messages, then a threat.

Trenn's rule returned with the steadiness of his thumb tapping once against his cup. One word, then stop.

He had taught them to be Nell and Bash on the roads. In the Regent's bounded system, a given name was one line, a family name another, a recognized home a third. One line let a searcher narrow the hunt. All three let a skilled living user reach deeper.

Nell had watched that reach happen at Willa Corst's house. A Regent officer laid a living palm on the copper plate beside the door. His magic traveled through the fittings, and the beams recited the record they had been made to store.

“Willa Corst,” the house said in Willa's own exhausted voice. “The red-doored home above the eastern salt cuts.”

Willa had covered her ears. She had still been Willa after the words were stolen, furious and frightened and entirely herself, but the officer had possessed a road into her life.

Later, Indexer Prax offered Nell a bargain beneath three shelves of silent ledgers.

“His family line and his home,” Prax said. “Give me those, and I will put you through the Gate.”

Prax had living hands, living magic, and the patient smile of someone asking a child to price her brother. The ledgers merely held what people like him fed them.

Nell had refused because she did not know Bash's missing lines. She would have refused if she had known.

Now she had built a smaller ledger for the entire internet.

Celia found her at two in the morning sorting facts into columns.

PUBLIC: the night Bash insisted they watch the moonrise and won by eleven minutes; the broken roofs at Drosswall; the existence of Trenn's token.

PRIVATE: the silver button sewn inside Trenn's collar; the ash-hound scar that bent Bash's little finger; three taps, a pause, and two for *Still alive?*; one tap for *For now*.

PRIVATE: Saint bit the customs priest because Nell fed the mule the tasseled end of Bash's red scarf to keep him quiet. Saint objected when the priest tried to take it back.

Celia set a mug beside the laptop. “Someone emailed me a picture of our front steps.”

Nell's fingers stopped.

“I believe something happened to you,” Celia said. “I believe you lost people. I don't know how to believe every part of it, but I know these strangers are hurting you. Please close the post.”

At the hospital, a doctor had called Bash an organizing figure in an extended trauma narrative. The phrase offered Nell a terrible kind of rest. If Bash was a symptom, she could stop waiting without abandoning him. She would only be getting well.

Then she remembered him in the dark between Drosswall walls, tapping three-pause-two through the stone until her shaking slowed.

Nell deleted every searchable clue from the post. She left the title and a contact form. Anyone who answered would receive a question in private, and the answer would not be something they could steal from her page.

It was less proof. It was also the first protection she had ever built that left Bash a choice about entering it.

## June 7

The message arrived at 8:16 in the morning.

> Saint bit the customs priest because you fed him my red scarf. Also, the small moon rose first because you were wrong, not because it liked you better.

Nell read it six times. Then she carried the laptop to Celia without taking her eyes off the screen.

Hope was not warm. It was a trapdoor opening under her ribs. Anyone could have watched her old interviews before she deleted them. Anyone could have guessed that a mule bit someone. But no public version mentioned the scarf, or Nell's part in sacrificing it, or Bash's three-day sulk over losing it.

They answered through the relay.

Which hand?

> Left. Little finger. You set it crooked and blamed the ash-hound.

What did Trenn hide inside his collar?

> A silver button he claimed was lucky after it failed to be valuable.

Three. Pause. Two.

> One. For now.

Nell's hands shook so badly Celia had to steady the laptop.

Bash wrote that he had left a cello lesson that morning and vanished for twelve seconds. He returned in the same red scarf, carrying 617 days of scars and one half of a copper token. When he searched the only phrase he thought Nell might have used, he found a post four months old.

He sent a photograph of that morning's date beside the copper crescent, then appeared live on camera so Celia could see that the bent finger moved when he moved it. He looked younger than Nell remembered and older than any twelve-year-old had permission to look. Behind him, two adults hovered with the rigid helplessness Nell recognized from Celia.

“We never told each other our dates,” Nell typed.

> We gave the Gate separate memories. The resistance built the charge around each traveler's remembered departure. It must have returned each of us to our own anchor.

Not the Regent's identity lines. Not a rule for every crossing. This one Gate had shaped what their living memories supplied, and their memories had never matched.

Nell had spent four months treating absence as evidence of death. Instead, she had been waiting for a departure that had not happened yet. The thought was so unreasonable it fitted the facts better than anything reasonable had.

They did not exchange surnames. They did not type exact homes into a channel that had already attracted thieves. Celia joined a video call with the frightened adults behind Bash, and the adults arranged the rest.

The children agreed to meet at 30th Street Station.

## 30th Street Station

Nell recognized Bash by the way he distrusted the building.

He stood beneath the departure board with his back against a stone column. His eyes counted exits before faces. His left shoulder stayed angled away from the crowd, guarding an injury that no longer needed guarding.

He looked twelve.

That was almost worse than seeing a stranger. Ravel had lengthened him, sharpened his cheeks, and put gray in the expression around his eyes. The Gate had restored his departure body and his whole red scarf. It had not restored ignorance.

The scarf's tasseled end was perfect again. Nell remembered Saint chewing it to wet red threads, and grief rose for the ridiculous missing damage. Bash had been given back the cloth. Neither of them had been given back the person who wore it before Ravel.

Celia stopped several steps behind Nell. Two adults waited on Bash's side of the concourse. None of them called the children forward.

Bash took out a copper crescent.

Nell held up hers.

The broken edges met. Trenn's scratched sun became one badly proportioned circle.

Bash raised his left hand. The little finger leaned toward the next one. A pale line crossed his wrist where a Drosswall arrow had glanced from glass and found skin. Nell showed him the matching white hook in her palm.

Still he did not smile.

He tapped three times against the token, waited, then tapped twice.

Nell answered once.

For now.

The distance between them disappeared. Bash hit her like an undersized landslide, arms locked around her shoulders, face jammed against her hoodie. Nell held on until the station stopped tilting.

He smelled of train dust and laundry soap instead of woodsmoke. His shoulder blades were too small beneath her hands. Nell had wanted proof that the boy from Ravel existed; holding him made her understand that both versions did, layered together, and neither canceled the other.

Then he pulled back and said, “Did the path break, or did you cut it?”

She could have lied. He had earned more than evidence.

“I used the severance line.”

His hands dropped. “You let me think the crack took it.”

“I did. I should have corrected you the first time you said it. I was afraid you'd hate me—and that you'd make the Gate our next mission. That was wrong.”

“I needed the truth from you.”

“I know.”

“And I told you I could stabilize it.”

“The Regent was at your neck.”

“I needed five seconds.”

“You had none.”

People rolled suitcases around them. The departure board clicked through ordinary delays. No adult stepped into the space where Ravel stood between the children.

Bash looked toward his family and then away. “Tavra is still there. Saint. Everyone whose jar we opened. If the Gate can be reached again—”

“No.” The word came out in Trenn's road voice: one piece, then stop.

“You don't get to make that choice alone too.”

“If I hadn't cut it, the Regent could have followed your memory straight here.”

“I know what the risk was.”

“Then why are we arguing?”

“Because you decided my risk belonged to you.”

The *too* found its mark. Nell heard Indexer Prax asking her to make Bash useful. She heard resistance leaders praising children because children could remember a departure with painful clarity. She heard Bash turning survival into the next mission before either of them had learned how to sleep in beds again.

She stepped toward the nearest exit.

Celia's face tightened, but she stayed where she was. For months Nell had complained that adults never trusted her account. Now her mother trusted her enough not to rescue her from an argument only she could finish.

“Nell.” Bash did not grab her. “I can't promise I won't look for a route.”

She stopped.

“I can't promise I'll help you,” she said.

“I know.” His voice roughened. “But if one appears, neither of us opens it, enters it, or cuts it without the other knowing. No emergency rule unless there is actually an emergency.”

“There was actually an emergency.”

“Then your decision was right and still hurt me.”

Nell hated that sentence because it left no clean side to stand on.

She came back to the matched token. All her months of searching had been built from what she refused to give. The refusal had kept them safe. It did not have to be the only thing keeping them together.

“Nell Mercado,” she said. “Philadelphia. A narrow brick rowhouse in Frankford, with a blue drainpipe and trains that shake the spoons at night.”

Bash let out a breath.

“Mercado,” he repeated, not taking it, only receiving it.

Then he said, “Sebastian Wren. Cambridge. Second-floor apartment over a violin repair shop, back room, radiator knocks in threes.” His mouth twitched. The fuller version—Sebastian “Bash” Wren—had the stiff absurdity of a school form, but Nell held every part of it.

“Wren,” Nell said.

Nothing flashed. No copper warmed. No hidden system tightened around them. The names rested in ordinary station air because two people had chosen to put them there.

Bash separated the token halves and returned hers.

“No unilateral choices,” Nell said.

“Shared bad decisions only.”

“That is not what I said.”

This time, he smiled.

## One Year After Nell Returned

Reunion had not taught either of them to sleep normally.

Bash still chose the floor when a room had only one door. Nell still hid crackers in coat pockets. Their families argued about missed school, train fares, and whether the Gate pack under Bash's bed counted as preparation or obsession. Joint therapy gave the children better words for some things and no agreement at all about Ravel.

They learned to ask before checking each other's scars. They learned that a slammed cupboard could ruin an afternoon and that ruining an afternoon did not ruin a week. Bash visited Philadelphia; Nell visited Cambridge. Sometimes they fought about the Gate until one of them missed a train. Sometimes they watched terrible movies and spoke of Ravel only to complain that no modern pizza used enough root pepper.

The two copper halves stayed separate. That was not distrust. It was the shape of the promise.

On the anniversary, they went back to the supermarket.

The automatic doors opened. Nell stopped on the rubber mat.

Freezer air reached her from aisle nine. For an instant she had glass-light in her eyes and Bash's fingers leaving her wrist. She counted the front doors, the staff door, the fire exit beyond produce, the loading corridor—fast, alone, breath thinning.

The store smelled of floor wax and oranges. A cart wheel knocked in an uneven rhythm. Nobody else noticed that the threshold could become a cliff, which meant nobody else could cross it for her.

Bash waited outside the threshold. He did not touch her.

“Want company?” he asked.

Nell looked at the store map. “You take the back two.”

He counted them. Then he tapped three-pause-two against the cart handle, a question offered instead of demanded.

She answered once.

They went to aisle nine. Bash chose pepperoni. Nell said Ravel root rounds had tasted better, which was untrue and made him accuse her of rewriting history. They argued until Celia told them to put one pizza in the cart or eat crackers for dinner.

Nell chose one. Bash shared the exit count.

They walked out together through ordinary doors.

illustrations.alt: Under the small blue moon, the bright path snaps as Bash still grips Nell's wrist at the Glass Gate.
Thirteen again, Nell braces against a freezer, her old tally belt looping twice around her waist.
Celia asks Nell to close the public post while Nell sits motionless at the kitchen laptop.
As Nell trembles after Bash's private replies, Celia steadies the laptop on the table.
Bash buries his face against Nell's hoodie as they hold each other in the station concourse.
Nell turns toward the station exit while Bash calls without reaching for her; Celia stays back.
After sharing their full names, Nell and Bash hold separate copper halves as Bash finally smiles.
At the supermarket doorway, Nell answers Bash's tap on the cart handle while he gives her room.

editions.title: The Weight of Falling Up
editions.body:
# The Weight of Falling Up

By the time Examiner Dovek called my name, three people had already left the roof. Two had chosen brooms, which was what sensible people at Nine Eaves usually did.

The first leaned low over a broom and cut around the western chimney in a polished brown arc. The second sat upright on another, rising at a measured angle while the lacquered handle stayed level beneath both hands. The third went past between the lifted wings of a pale horse, hands buried in its mane while each downstroke sent a warm gust rolling over the slates.

Two brooms were not a coincidence. Nine Eaves kept racks of practice models, broom-width gates, and enough standard diagrams to wallpaper a tower. The horse was rare enough to draw looks in the dining hall, but not questions on an assessment roof. Its lane was painted wider, its harness had already passed inspection, and everyone present knew what those wings could do.

Then there was me.

“Juni Wex,” Dovek called again.

“Present. Still regrettably attached to the building.”

The Collegium of Nine Eaves occupied most of the view below us: black roofs pitched at improbable angles, bridges stitching tower to tower, windows bright as chips of amber. Beyond it, the city fell away in terraces toward a silver bend of river. The launch roof was so high that birds passed beneath the gutters. Prestige, I had learned, was often ordinary terror with excellent masonry.

I sat on the warm slate and unlaced my shoes. Mine were scuffed brown leather, bought without enchantment, one still bearing a pale water mark from a badly judged fountain.

I pulled them off, set my stockinged feet on the roof, and turned the right shoe heel-up across my knee.

Dovek crouched opposite me. Their examination coat snapped once in the wind and settled. “Begin.”

The ink stylus came from my cuff. I pressed its blunt nib beside the heel and drew the first stroke in a curve around the back of the shoe. The second hooked across the underside toward the arch. The third doubled inward, a black curl aimed at the small hollow between them. It looked less like a word than an arrow teaching the wind where to leave.

Nothing happened. Ink was only ink until someone living asked more of it.

I cupped the shoe between both hands, breathed, and let warmth run out through my palms. The three lines drank it. For an instant, black deepened beyond black.

I drew the mirrored wind curl around the other heel and underside, charged it, and put both shoes back on. My fingers trembled at the laces. Apparently fear was mostly an audience with opinions.

Dovek tapped one gloved finger above the right-hand curl. “No crown.”

“I’m fond of steering.”

“And your stationary count?”

“Small bursts.”

I traced the shape I had omitted: a shallow cap with three points. “A crown spreads one heel’s wind beneath my center. It will check a fall and quiet a turn, but it cannot steer. Once I feed it power, one point burns away per breath. Three points, exactly three breaths, then the crown is gone and the narrow jet returns.”

“Can you interrupt it?”

“I can cut power, but the unused points burn out anyway. It cannot be restarted.”

“A limitation.”

“A feature with strict opinions about counting.”

“A limitation,” Dovek repeated. “You are required to remain inside the stationary boundary for a count of three. Demonstrate the limitation. Do not conceal it.”

The first broom candidate flashed past the far eave, coat streaming straight behind. Above, the second held almost motionless while the broom’s bristles trembled through corrections too small to see. The pale horse climbed through a patch of sun, every feather briefly edged in gold.

I imagined a wide, blunt plume roaring beneath me while I hung unable to turn, all three crown points visibly burning away. Effective, temporary, and about as elegant as being held aloft by an argument.

“Understood,” I said.

I did understand. I simply had no intention of doing it.

* * *

Dovek raised a hand.

I ran for the edge.

At the gutter, I jumped, pointed both soles down, and drove warmth through my legs.

The curls answered.

Two pale streams of wind tore from my heels. They snapped my coat against my back, flung grit from the gutter, and punched me upward so hard my stomach arrived a moment after the rest of me.

I made a sound that began as a scream and improved into laughter.

The shoes did not carry me. The ink did not decide where I went. I supplied the power; the curls narrowed it into two rushing jets; my feet aimed the result. With both soles turned toward the roof and the output matched, I climbed. When I swept my heels behind me, the streams bent backward and shoved me forward into the blue.

For three glorious seconds, everything worked.

Then I drove a shade too much power through my left leg. Its jet surged harder.

My left hip lifted. My right shoulder dropped. The western chimney tipped sideways in front of me as I rolled toward the weaker stream.

“Excellent,” I told the rapidly rotating school. “A view.”

I nearly answered by forcing more through both heels. Instead I eased my left leg and fed the right until the two pale currents matched. The roll slowed. I opened my arms, shifted my hips, and came level with enough dignity to fool anyone who had not seen the first half.

The course turned around a tall iron arch strung with blue streamers. The first broom candidate banked through it by leaning into the curved handle. The second rose in a straight, measured line, hands quiet on the grip. Higher still, the winged horse folded its wings for one clean heartbeat, then opened them and surged upward.

There are respectable ways to fly. I had watched them practiced from the lower courts for years: the long broom bank, the patient broom hover, the powerful bargain between a rider and a winged animal. They all looked as though the sky were a country one might enter with the correct papers.

I arrived with two handwritten winds shouting at my heels.

I angled both feet down and poured on a smooth, sustained rush. Bells chimed somewhere below, nine notes thrown loose among the roofs. The jets curled white around my ankles and streamed behind me in twisting ribbons. Every change began in my body: toes lowered for climb, heels swept back for speed, one ankle canted outward to carve the bank. The air struck my soles, seized my coat, watered my eyes. I did not feel weightless. I felt gloriously outvoted by my own momentum.

The blue streamers cracked beside my ears. The city wheeled below in slate and copper and green garden squares. My legs began to tremble from holding both channels even, but the strain had a rhythm: power, angle, answer; power, angle, answer.

At the top of the arch hung the high-course bell.

I pitched forward, let the paired streams drive me through a rising curve, and slapped the bell with my palm.

Its note burst out bright enough to shake my teeth.

The arch rushed past beneath me. I was still climbing and moving far too fast toward the next roofline.

I swung both heels ahead and gave a moderate reverse pulse.

Wind blasted forward across my soles. My speed eased. The jets rasped over the curls and carried a few black flecks away into the white stream.

I noticed. I also noticed that the course marker remained safely unstruck, which seemed the more flattering observation.

Below, Dovek wrote on the examination sheet. Naturally, I assumed it meant *astonishing, perhaps historic*.

The stationary boundary waited ahead.

* * *

It was a square of yellow ribbons stretched between four slender poles on neighboring roofs, enclosing a piece of perfectly good empty air. The second broom candidate already occupied it.

They sat upright in the center, the broom level beneath them. Its bound twigs made tiny, practiced corrections while Dovek counted from the launch roof below.

“One.”

The rider shifted one knee. The broom eased back half a handspan.

“Two.”

The bristles dipped and recovered. From a distance, the candidate might have been sitting on a bench.

“Three.”

They glided out with a small, satisfied turn.

I hovered outside the ribbons on a low sustained rush. My legs had opinions now. Both were unprintable.

The safe answer waited in my cuff. I could draw the three-point crown over one heel, feed it power, and let the broad plume spend its three breaths beneath my center. I would lose steering while it burned, but I would remain stable long enough for the count.

Instead, I entered the square and began firing alternating microbursts.

Left, right, left, right. Each gust lasted barely longer than a blink. My ankles chattered beneath me as I corrected every drift with another sharp pulse. If I moved quickly enough, I reasoned, I would appear almost still.

“One,” Dovek called.

A left burst nudged me toward the upper ribbon. I snapped the right heel down and inward. Its jet kicked me back, then too far. Black specks peppered the pale wind behind it.

The first broom candidate swept along the outer course. The second left the square on an easy level line. The pale horse crossed the sun above, the rider bent to its rhythm. All three were moving. Moving looked dignified.

“Two.”

I fired right, left, right in quick succession. Each ignition punched through my calf. The last correction spun me a quarter turn and produced a sound from my throat like a startled kettle.

I smiled toward Dovek. Dovek did not smile back.

The right curl was shedding more ink than the left. I favored that foot whenever I drifted, and the separate little starts were eating its edges. I twisted enough to glimpse the heel. A gray nick had appeared in the outer curve.

“Three.”

I lurched out of the square with my chest heaving. Behind me, the wind-traces knotted and unraveled in no pattern worth admitting to.

“Juni,” Dovek called.

I curved back toward the nearest eave. Dovek had crossed to its ridge, the examination sheet tucked under one arm. Their attention fixed on my right heel.

“Your outer channel is scouring.”

So much for altitude protecting a person’s secrets.

“It has another descent in it.”

“You may declare a repair pause. One-point deduction. Inspect both shoes, then continue.”

One point. A small price, if points were the only things being weighed. But the other candidates were clean silhouettes against the sky, and I was sweating hard enough to drown a modest insect. A repair on the ridge would make the runes look provisional. It would make them look like something I had drawn on ordinary leather that morning.

Which, inconveniently, they were.

The rooftop-survey roster closed today. I pictured a term copying elevations from other apprentices’ notebooks while they measured the world with their own eyes.

I raised my right heel and looked. The nick was pale, narrow, and entirely real.

“I can complete,” I said.

Dovek’s expression did not change, but their questions became precise when they were worried. “Have you measured how much line remains?”

“I have seen it.”

“That was not my question.”

I fed a thin stream through the right curl. It came half a beat late, ragged at one edge.

“It is enough.”

The words left a sour place behind my teeth.

Dovek held my gaze for another beat, then pointed toward the descending course and the white landing ring on the launch roof.

“Proceed.”

* * *

I proceeded too quickly.

Smooth, matched output would have worn the ink slowly. I managed several sensible seconds of it.

Then I saw the first broom candidate arrowing toward the landing roof below, and my good judgment, already bruised, developed a competitive fever.

I tipped my heels back and drove.

The paired jets lengthened into white cords. Roofs rose around me. Wind shoved hair into my mouth. I spat it out, rolled between two stone finials, and added a sharp right pulse to recover the line. The pale horse wheeled well above the course, kept to its familiar wider lane. The second broom glided toward the far landing mark with infuriating composure.

My own ring came into view: a white circle on dark slate, Dovek approaching along the ridge beside it. I was high and fast. I should have begun braking then, with both feet angled forward and a long, moderate reverse flow.

Instead I chased the lost seconds.

The ring widened below.

I swung both heels ahead and drove power through the curls.

The left jet roared forward.

The right gave one ragged cough. Reverse wind tore across the worn outer curve, lifted the last thread of black, and silenced it.

The left side of my body was shoved backward. The right kept carrying forward and down.

My right shoulder dropped. The city rolled over me. In one sickening instant I snapped into a rightward corkscrew.

I forced more power down both legs by instinct.

Only the left answered.

The surviving reverse jet hammered my left side farther back. The corkscrew tightened. Roof, sky, roof, sky—the world became a wheel with me badly nailed to its rim.

I tried again. More power. More spin.

The shoes had not betrayed me. The right curl had announced its wear in black dust and a gray break. Dovek had offered me time. I had spent both warnings to purchase the appearance of ease.

“Call your stop, Juni!” Dovek shouted.

One hand was raised at the roof’s edge, ready for my declared surrender.

I could call and fail cleanly. I would be alive, unqualified, and indoors for a term.

Or I could keep feeding the one jet I had because motion felt more useful than falling.

That was the trap. The left curl was obeying perfectly. Every desperate command made the imbalance worse.

There was no graceful way out.

That helped.

Grace was what had put me here.

I cut all power.

The left jet vanished. Nothing corrected me; nothing chose a safer line. The added torque stopped, but the spin remained, and gravity took the rest.

I fell.

* * *

Wind clawed tears from my eyes. The roofs below looked small enough to fit in a box.

I pulled my knees tight, not to slow the rotation but to bring the failed shoe within reach. The world became a smaller, faster wheel around one steady thing: the scuffed heel a handspan from my nose.

The outer curl had opened to bare brown leather.

I tore the stylus from my cuff.

With the shoe turning beside my face, I dragged the missing curve around the heel. The nib skated. I drew again, slower, following the surviving line under the shoe until wet black joined black.

The base curl was whole.

I could have powered it then and hoped two narrow jets would agree before I struck a roof. Hope had already submitted enough examination work for one morning.

Above the repaired curl, I drew a shallow cap.

One point.

The roofs spun through the corner of my sight.

Two.

The pale horse crossed the wheel of sky, wings spread wide.

Three.

The crown waited in fresh black ink.

Neither leather nor drawing knew I was falling. Neither could decide to help. I flattened my palm over the heel and sent my living warmth through every new line.

Then I extended the right leg beneath me and supplied power.

The crowned curl opened.

Instead of a narrow jet kicking from one heel, a broad pale plume curved inward and blossomed beneath my center. It had no aim beyond the shape I had drawn. It could not choose the roof or turn me toward it. It simply poured wide and steady while I held the power.

I took the first breath.

The first crown point flashed white and blew away. The broad wind pressed against my rotation from below. Roof and sky stopped striking past quite so fast. My corkscrew widened, shuddered, and began to flatten.

One.

I took the second breath.

The next point burned. The plume thickened around my falling body, opposing the drop without erasing it. My stomach rose against my ribs. I opened from the tuck and hauled my left heel into view.

Its curl was frayed nearly through.

Two.

I drew the third breath.

The last point brightened above my right heel.

I put the stylus to the left shoe. Around the outside curve, under the heel, into the channel. Quick but whole. My lungs strained to release the breath too soon. I held it long enough to press my thumb over the wet line and send warmth into the repair.

The left curl darkened.

The final crown point vanished.

Three.

The broad plume collapsed to a narrow right-hand stream. I cut it at once rather than let one-sided thrust start another turn. The crown was gone, its one use spent, but the repaired curl beneath it remained.

For one raw heartbeat I was falling between decisions.

Then I aimed both heels below me and fed them equal power.

Two clean streams struck the air.

My hips steadied between them. I canted both feet against what remained of the turn and let the matched thrust unwind it. Then I angled both soles together and climbed away from the roofs on a smooth white rush.

“Right rune wore through!” I shouted toward Dovek. My voice tore thin in the wind. “I saw the damage. I declined the repair.”

The admission sounded embarrassingly small.

It also sounded true.

I did not chase the time I had lost. I did not rattle through frantic corrections. I held both outputs low and even, let the wind show every adjustment, and took the long curve back toward the landing roof.

The first broom candidate circled wide of my path. The second watched from beyond the yellow square, broom almost level. The pale horse beat upward with the rider low against its neck.

And I flew.

Not like any of them. Not tidily. My renewed jets streamed behind Nine Eaves, wavering when my ankles tired and straightening when I trusted the balance between them. A crosswind shoved me; I tilted both soles and let the paired thrust answer. Speed pulled me forward; I eased power instead of hiding it beneath another burst.

The landing ring swelled below.

I began braking while it still looked too far away.

Both heels forward. Both curls fed gently.

The jets streamed ahead in two pale fans, pushing against my motion. Ink flecks lifted from them, but slowly now, without the violent black spray of the earlier brake. The force climbed through my ankles, knees, and hips. I let it.

The roof rose.

I turned both soles down for one last soft rush, cut power, and dropped the final handspan onto slate.

Both ordinary shoes landed inside the white ring.

Momentum carried me three stumbling paces. I windmilled, recovered, and remained upright.

For several seconds, this seemed an unreasonable amount of success.

Then my legs sat me down.

* * *

Dovek came to stand at the edge of the ring.

I lay on my back with my knees up. “If that was the posture component, I request a merciful interpretation.”

“Your stationary-control component failed.”

“Ah.”

“You identified visible wear and declined an offered repair pause.”

“I remember that less fondly.”

“You continued into a high-load reverse brake without an adequate margin.”

“Are we approaching a point?” I asked.

“We are circling it to ensure you recognize the terrain.”

I pushed myself upright. Both heels were visible beyond my knees: the base curls dark and whole, the right crown entirely gone, the leather around them scuffed and dusty. They looked homemade because I had made them. They looked temporary because they were. Neither fact seemed shameful from the ground.

Dovek crouched and set the sheet on the slate between us.

“You also diagnosed asymmetric thrust while under load,” they said. “You stopped feeding it. You restored both channels without external intervention, used the crown as declared, stated the fault, and completed a controlled landing.”

The wind lifted one corner of the paper.

Beside *stationary control*, Dovek had written a mark I did not enjoy.

Beside *judgment under failure*, they had written one I did.

At the bottom was a pass.

I read it twice, in case the second reading revealed an educational cruelty.

“The rooftop-survey practicum?” I asked.

“You are qualified.”

Dovek held up a finger before I could become unbearable. “For long crossings, you will carry enough physical margin to finish with half the drawing intact. You will set a declared repair threshold before launch. And you will not confuse hiding effort with demonstrating control.”

I looked at the failed mark beside the stationary component.

Earlier, I would have argued that mark upward. Now my calves were still shaking from three breaths inside my own wind.

“That seems fair,” I said.

Dovek gave me the sheet.

Out beyond the roof, the last traces of my flight were coming apart. The rapid bursts inside the yellow square had left a ragged knot freckled with black. Lower down, the corkscrew twisted through itself where one jet had overruled the other. Beneath it hung one broad pale bloom, already thinning at the edges.

From there to the landing ring, two clean ribbons arrived side by side.

I had wanted one smooth wake across the sky.

What remained was better: an honest record of the wind I had wasted, the wind I had trusted, and the moment I finally learned the difference.

illustrations.alt: Juni draws a black curl on a removed brown shoe while Dovek watches; both stockinged feet rest on slate.
Juni approaches the iron arch on two heel jets beside two broom candidates and a rider on a winged pale horse.
Inside four yellow ribbons, Juni tilts as a right-heel burst throws pale wind and black ink flecks.
Juni raises a worn right heel beside the eave while Dovek watches from the ridge with the sheet under one arm.
Juni corkscrews as only the left heel blasts wind forward; Dovek raises a gloved hand from the roof edge.
Juni presses a thumb to the repaired left shoe while the last point above the right heel feeds a broad plume over distant roofs.
Juni lands with both shoes inside the white ring, knees bending and arms spread, heel winds extinguished.
Juni holds the sheet beside Dovek and looks out at fading tangled winds, a broad bloom and two clean ribbons reaching the roof.
